newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish Islamic schools fear army-inspired closure.
newsitem.headline: Turkish Islamic schools fear army-inspired closure.

text.p: Headscarved girl pupils scribbled notes over metal desks on Monday at an Islamic secondary schools where teachers and parents fear closure in a row between Turkey's army and government.
The generals have ordered a cut in the number of "Imam Hatip" schools they say are breeding grounds for the next generation of Islamist activists.
The army's demand, part of a crackdown it wants Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan to impose, has cast a cloud over an Imam Hatip on the outskirts of Ankara.
"Parents are calling us to ask if the school is going to be closed, they are very concerned," said the headteacher, who asked that he and his school not be named.
Behind him a cardboard frieze with the word "Allah" inscribed on it in Arabic and Turkish scripts hung on the wall.
The military in February told the government to impose eight years of compulsory secularist education on children, from the current five.
Under the proposed changes, the number of pupils at religious schools would drop, forcing the eventual closure of many Imam Hatips.
Children would only be able to go to religious schools after the age of 15, when they would already be formed in the secularist mould.
"The children are worried as well. They are frightened the authorities will tell them one day that the police or gendarmerie have closed the school and locked the gate," the headteacher said.
Erbakan has yet to take action to water down religious education, a key issue for him. But he is under pressure from his secularist coalition allies to carry out the army's wishes.
Many supporters and members of Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party are graduates of Imam Hatips, including several cabinet ministers and Istanbul mayor Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
But every government since the late 1940s -- even three military administrations -- has presided over an increase in the number of Imam Hatips opened.

"Because the Welfare Party is in government now, they are saying Imam Hatips create people for Welfare," said Fehmi Calmuk, head of a former pupils' association. "They are trying to put this issue in a pigeon hole," he said.
The schools have gone beyond their original remit of training Moslem clergy and now teach far more children than can be employed in the mosques.
Almost 500,000 pupils attend 561 Imam Hatips, which have a reputation for discipline and a solid grounding in non-religious subjects.
